newsitem.title: POLAND: Pope tells huge crowd of Poles to nurture freedom.
newsitem.headline: Pope tells huge crowd of Poles to nurture freedom.

text.p: Pope John Paul told a crowd of more than a million Poles on Sunday that now that they had regained freedom after nearly half a century of communism they should use it to spread love and truth.

The Pope attracted the biggest crowd of his trip so far when a sea of people turned out to see him at the Blonia park in Krakow, the city where he lived for more than 20 years as priest, bishop and cardinal.

The "homecoming" attracted more than 1.5 million people, according to Polish Government Protection Office (UOP) security officials at the scene. Thousands of banners went up in the 48- hectare field as the Pope was driven through the crowd in a glass-topped popemobile.

The 77-year-old Roman Catholic leader spoke in a strong voice at the mass, which took place the day after Saturday's packed agenda of four events that brought him from his beloved Tatra mountains to Krakow, the last leg of his 11-day-tour.
Wearing resplendent gold robes billowing in a soft breeze, he told the crowd that 10 years ago "we had before us the problem of the discovery of freedom".

In 1987, the country was still run by communists. Two years later in 1989 they gave way to Eastern Europe's first democratically-elected government, headed by the Solidarity trade union, which the Pope unflaggingly backed.
To the Pope's joy after years of praying for a more united Europe, the domino-like fall of the Soviet bloc was under way.
"Now divine providence is putting a new task before us: to love and serve. To love in deed and in truth," he said speaking from a flower-bedecked altar platform overlooking the expanse.

How Poles should use their freedom in the post-communist era has been the thread running through the Pope's speeches on the trip, his seventh to Poland, which ends on Tuesday when he returns to the Vatican.

Before the mass John Paul had a brief meeting with Polish Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz at the Krakow Archbishop's residence. Asked by Cimoszewicz in front of reporters how his trip was going, the Pope replied "fine".
The prime minister, a former communist, said later that he had told the Pope "He should be full of optimism, because we will cope with the problems that we have."
At the mass the Pope canonised Queen Jadwiga, who died in 1399 at the age of 25 after helping to spread Christianity to neighbouring countries, particularly Lithuania.

He prayed that the example of the new saint, whom Poles have venerated for centuries as a holy woman and benefactor of the arts and education, would teach the nation "what it means to love in deed and in truth, what it means to be truly free".

During the trip, a sentimental journey through some of the areas of his youth, he warned Poles of a moral wilderness and the pitfalls of a get-rich-quick mentality as the once-centralised economy soars to new heights.
He has pulled no punches on some of the most burning issues dividing them, most notably abortion.
He has bluntly told his countrymen that economically and culturally successful societies were nothing more than barbarian if they allowed it.

Whether abortion should remain liberalised or be restricted again is a key issue in campaigning for September's elections, in which a powerful alliance centred around the pro-Catholic Solidarity union is rivalling the ruling ex-communists.

The Pope also has warned of a new wall of economic and political selfishness that he said had arisen in Europe and was threatening the unity of the continent just as much as the Berlin Wall did before communism's fall.
